sophistry
The use of clever but false arguments, especially with the intention of deceiving people in formal debate.
The politician relied on clever sophistry to divert attention away from the glaring budget deficit.
pusillanimous
Lacking courage or determination when facing difficult decisions, danger, or opposition in public life.
The committee condemned the director's pusillanimous decision to abandon the project at the first sign of opposition.
recrudescence
A sudden revival or renewed outbreak of an unwanted condition, disease, or period of political unrest.
Health authorities warned that a recrudescence of the infection could occur if vaccination rates declined.
ineluctable
Unable to be avoided, evaded, or changed despite all attempts to alter the eventual course of events.
The decline of the old industrial district seemed ineluctable as modern technology transformed the local economy.
palimpsest
A manuscript or piece of writing material on which later writing has been superimposed on effaced earlier traces.
The historic city centre is a fascinating palimpsest where medieval streets coexist with modern architecture.
apotheosis
The highest point in the development of something, or the elevation of a person to divine status.
Winning the prestigious international award marked the apotheosis of her long and distinguished academic career.
synecdoche
A figure of speech in which a part is made to represent the whole or vice versa.
Using the phrase all hands on deck is a classic example of synecdoche in literary analysis.
metonymy
The substitution of the name of an attribute or adjunct for that of the thing meant.
Referring to the executive branch of the government as Downing Street is a common use of metonymy.
anomie
A lack of usual social or ethical standards in an individual or group during rapid societal change.
Sociologists argued that economic instability created widespread anomie among young workers across the country.
liminal
Relating to a transitional or initial stage of a process, occupying a position at a boundary.
Adolescence is often described as a liminal period when young people transition from childhood into adulthood.
interstitial
Situated within or relating to small narrow spaces or gaps between things in a larger structure.
The researcher studied the interstitial spaces between cellular walls under an advanced electronic microscope.
overweening
Showing excessive, exaggerated, or arrogant confidence or pride that ignores reasonable advice or warnings from others.
His overweening ambition caused him to alienate his closest allies during the election campaign.
captious
Tending to find petty faults or raise trivial objections in order to confuse or annoy other people.
The examiner made captious remarks about minor formatting details rather than addressing the core arguments.
tendentious
Expressing or intending to promote a particular opinion or point of view, especially a controversial one.
The documentary was criticised for presenting a tendentious account of the historic conflict.
meretricious
Apparently attractive or appealing on the surface but having in reality no value, integrity, or substance.
The reviewer dismissed the novel as a meretricious exercise in flashy style without emotional depth.
rebarbative
Unattractive, objectionable, or repellent in appearance, tone, or general character to those who encounter it.
The official adopted a rebarbative tone that quickly discouraged citizens from asking further questions.
ameliorate
To make a bad or unsatisfactory situation better, more tolerable, or easier to endure for everyone.
The council introduced community programmes to ameliorate housing conditions in the inner city.
obfuscate
To deliberately make something obscure, unclear, or difficult to understand, especially during public discussions.
The spokesperson attempted to obfuscate the facts by using complicated financial jargon.
cogent
Clear, logical, and convincing to the intellect when presented in a formal speech or written argument.
She presented a cogent case for reform that persuaded even the most sceptical board members.
germane
Relevant and appropriate to a subject or topic currently under consideration in a discussion or study.
Please ensure that all questions asked during the seminar are germane to the topic.
salient
Most noticeable, prominent, or important among a collection of features, facts, or observations in analysis.
The report summarised the salient points of the proposal in a clear two-page executive summary.
panacea
A solution or remedy for all difficulties or diseases, often expected but rarely achievable in practice.
Technology is a powerful tool for education, but it is not a panacea for all learning challenges.
hegemony
Leadership or dominant influence exercised by one nation, social group, or authority over others in a system.
The empire maintained its regional hegemony through economic trade alliances and diplomatic influence.
anachronism
A thing, person, or custom belonging or appropriate to a period other than that in which it exists.
Using a quill pen in a modern software office felt like an amusing anachronism to the visitors.
verisimilitude
The appearance or semblance of being true, authentic, or real within artistic, literary, or theatrical representations.
Historical fiction requires a high degree of verisimilitude to convince readers of its setting.
vicissitude
An unwelcome or unexpected shift in circumstances or fortune during the course of a life or career.
Every successful business must learn to adapt to the unexpected vicissitude of the global marketplace.
epistemology
The branch of philosophy concerned with the nature, origin, scope, and limits of human knowledge.
Her research in epistemology focuses on how empirical evidence justifies scientific beliefs.
hermeneutics
The theory and methodology of interpretation, especially of scriptural, philosophical, or literary texts across historical periods.
Students of literature study hermeneutics to analyse how historical contexts shape text meanings.
paradigmatic
Serving as a typical, ideal, or standard pattern or model for a class of phenomena or ideas.
The breakthrough discovery became a paradigmatic example of collaborative scientific research in the modern era.
equivocate
To use ambiguous language intentionally in order to conceal the truth or avoid committing oneself to a position.
When questioned about the rising costs, the representative continued to equivocate rather than giving clear figures.
recalcitrant
Obstinately uncooperative towards authority or discipline, refusing to follow established rules or instructions given by leaders.
The recalcitrant student refused to participate in the group activity despite encouragement from the teacher.
intransigent
Unwilling or refusing to change one's views or to agree about something despite reasonable attempts at negotiation.
The dispute continued for weeks because both sides remained intransigent regarding contractual terms.
perfunctory
Carried out with a minimum of effort, care, or interest, purely as a routine or required duty.
He gave a perfunctory nod of greeting before returning immediately to his paperwork.
ineffable
Too great, intense, or beautiful to be expressed or described in ordinary human spoken or written words.
Standing atop the mountain peak filled her with an ineffable sense of wonder and peaceful stillness.
sycophant
A person who acts obsequiously towards someone important in order to gain advantage or personal influence.
The executive was surrounded by sycophant aides who praised every idea he mentioned.
alacrity
Brisk, cheerful, and enthusiastic readiness or promptness in responding to requests or performing tasks.
The volunteers accepted the challenge with alacrity and completed the preparations ahead of schedule.
insouciance
A relaxed and carefree attitude that shows freedom from anxiety, concern, or worry about consequences.
She faced the daunting exam with remarkable insouciance, confident in her months of preparation.
perspicacity
The quality of having ready insight into and understanding of complex matters or subtle distinctions.
Her political perspicacity allowed her to anticipate market shifts long before her competitors realised them.
pertinacious
Holding firmly to an opinion or a course of action with persistent and unyielding determination.
Through pertinacious research over several years, the team uncovered crucial historical documents.
supercilious
Behaving or looking as though one thinks one is superior to others, showing disdainful arrogance.
The supercilious smile on his face suggested he viewed the rest of the candidates with contempt.
dilettante
A person who cultivates an area of interest, such as the arts, without real commitment or knowledge.
Rather than committing to serious study, he remained a dilettante in several artistic disciplines.
paucity
The presence of something only in small or insufficient quantities or numbers; scarcity or relative lack.
The paucity of reliable evidence led the judge to dismiss the case before trial.
surfeit
An excessive amount or overabundant supply of something, often causing satiety, boredom, or mild disgust.
After weeks of continuous advertising campaigns, the audience suffered from a surfeit of promotional messages.
dissonance
A lack of agreement, harmony, or consistency between different elements, ideas, or musical notes.
There was a clear dissonance between the company's public statements and its actual workplace practices.
equivocal
Open to more than one interpretation, intentionally ambiguous, uncertain, or questionable in character or meaning.
The test results were equivocal, forcing the medical team to order additional examinations.
iconoclast
A person who attacks cherished beliefs or traditional institutions, challenging established social or cultural conventions.
As an artistic iconoclast, she constantly challenged traditional painting methods in her exhibitions.
cast aspersions on
To make critical or damaging remarks about someone's character, integrity, or reputation in public.
It is unfair to cast aspersions on her professional integrity without providing supporting evidence.
throw into sharp relief
To make a contrast, feature, or difficulty significantly more noticeable, clear, or prominent than before.
The crisis served to throw into sharp relief the existing flaws within the regional healthcare system.
bear testimony to
To provide clear proof, evidence, or confirmation of a particular truth, achievement, or historical fact.
The ancient stone monuments bear testimony to the sophisticated engineering skills of early civilisations.
lay the groundwork for
To make preliminary preparations or create the foundational conditions necessary for future success or development.
The preliminary research helped lay the groundwork for a major technological breakthrough in renewable energy.
